title: Rupee Slumps to 95.08 as Crude Tops $100 on US-Iran Escalation
excerpt: The currency fell 34 paise in a single session as Brent crude breached $100 for the first time in six weeks; analysts see a negative bias ahead.
body:
• The rupee slumped 34 paise to close at 95.08 against the US dollar on Wednesday — a provisional record-weak finish — as Brent crude surged past $100 a barrel.
  • The slide was driven by the US-Iran escalation: Washington destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday, and Tehran struck American targets in Jordan.
  • Weak equities and foreign fund outflows added pressure, though a soft dollar helped the rupee recover from an intraday low of 95.22.
  • Analysts expect the currency to trade with a negative bias while geopolitical risk keeps crude elevated.

The rupee slumped 34 paise to close at 95.08 (provisional) against the American currency on Wednesday, buckling as crude oil prices crossed the $100 per barrel mark and stoked concerns over inflation and heavy foreign-exchange outflows.

At the interbank foreign exchange market, the local unit opened at 94.80 — also its intraday high — before sliding to 95.22 as crude surged. It settled at 95.08, down from the previous close of 94.74, according to The Hindu.

Why the rupee fell

The proximate cause was geopolitical. Brent crude futures surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time in almost six weeks after attacks on oil facilities and ships in West Asia threatened to weaken an already strained supply chain amid US-Iran tensions. Brent was trading 2.94% higher at $100.73 a barrel.

"The rupee declined today due to rising crude oil prices and risk aversion in global markets," said Anuj Choudhary, research analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan. "Brent has breached the $100 mark following further escalation of tensions between the US and Iran. FII outflows also pressured the rupee. However, the rupee recovered its initial losses due to a weak dollar."

The escalation is concrete: the US military destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to attacks on its warships, and Iran hit back at American targets in Jordan. Weak domestic equities — the Sensex tanked 813 points on the day — and foreign institutional selling of ₹123.19 crore on Tuesday added to the pressure.

Dollar context

The dollar index, which gauges the greenback against six major currencies, was trading at 98.84, up just 0.05% — a relatively soft dollar that cushioned the rupee's fall from its intraday lows. The rupee's decline was thus less a dollar story than a crude-and-risk story.

What it means for NRIs

A weaker rupee cuts both ways for the diaspora. Remittances to India buy more rupees per dollar — good news for families receiving money home. But it raises the cost of everything India imports, from crude to electronics, feeding the inflation that erodes real returns on NRI deposits and India-focused portfolios.

"Escalation of geopolitical tensions between the US and Iran may also pressurise the rupee."

— Anuj Choudhary, Research Analyst, Mirae Asset Sharekhan

What to watch

Choudhary expects the local currency to trade with a negative bias on risk aversion and crude worries. The key variable is the US-Iran confrontation: any sign of de-escalation would likely pull Brent back below $100 and give the rupee breathing room. Until then, 95 to the dollar looks like the new normal — and further escalation could test weaker levels.
